title: Instance-wise Adaptive Scheduling via Derivative-Free Meta-Learning
claim: A meta-model learns a shared initialization via nested optimization, then adapts it per instance at test time.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; large meta-training block, small fine-tuning block, dashed feedback loops
description: The figure has two rounded containers. The large left one, Meta-Training, starts with an inset of two scatter-point Gaussian clouds. These show the parameter distribution moving along an orange ES-gradient arrow. Next to it, an initial parameter block θ0 feeds B colored instances drawn from a training instance set. The instances initialize stacked parameter copies in a yellow inner-loop box, which runs from θ(0) to θ(K). Dashed lines carry the results to a green outer-loop box. There, each instance's G and adapted θ(K) go through a function F, are summed, and form the Meta-Model ES Gradient. A dashed return arrow updates θ0. The small right panel, Fine-Tuning, takes the learned θ0* and a test instance Gt. It adapts θ over steps to produce a Solution. Pastel fills mark each component.
caption: overall framework of our method
abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning has achieved remarkable progress in solving NP-hard scheduling problems. However, existing methods primarily focus on optimizing average performance over training instances, overlooking the core objective of solving each individual instance with high quality. While several instance-wise adaptation mechanisms have been proposed, they are test-time approaches only and cannot share knowledge across different adaptation tasks. Moreover, they largely rely on gradient-based optimization, which could be ineffective in dealing with combinatorial optimization problems. We address the above issues by proposing an instance-wise meta-learning framework. It trains a meta model to acquire a generalizable initialization that effectively guides per-instance adaptation during inference, and overcomes the limitations of gradient-based methods by leveraging a derivative-free optimization scheme that is fully GPU parallelizable. Experimental results on representative scheduling problems demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing learning-based scheduling methods and instance-wise adaptation mechanisms under various task sizes and distributions.
